agent_notes: The superscription is verse 1 in the Hebrew numbering; the KJV counts it as verse 0 of its own chapter and starts verse 1 at the Hebrew verse 2. Every KJV number in this chapter is therefore one lower than the Hebrew.

The Rashi, Metzudat David and Meiri readings apply the psalm to Daniel in the lions' den. These commentaries are traditions about the psalm and are not found in the Hebrew text. I mention them in the commentary on verses 2, 6 and 8 only as the tradition, and I do not use them to shape the translation.

agent_notes: הִשְׂכִּילוּ is a perfect form, glossed by STEPBible as 'they will consider'. The sequence from וַיִּירְאוּ onward is past in form and future in sense; I rendered it as past in the literal layer and as the certain outcome in the dramatic one.

Reviewer request taken: יִשְׂמַח is an imperfect that may be read as a wish ('let the righteous rejoice', STEPBible) or as a prediction ('will rejoice'); וְחָסָה is a vav-perfect that continues it, not a separate wish. Token glosses 1, 4 and 6 now say 'will rejoice', 'and will take refuge', 'and will boast', matching the literal layer; the commentary names the jussive reading. I chose the predictive reading because the verse follows God's act in v. 8-10 as its result, and the vav-perfect continuation reads naturally as a statement; this is my own reading.
Radak's remark that the vav of וְחָסָה stands for 'when / because' (כי או כאשר) is an alternative construction; reported in the note on the verb and not adopted in the translations.
Rashi (Daniel) and Meiri identify the righteous man with Daniel, Meiri also saying the plain sense speaks of David himself. Mentioned as tradition, not asserted.

agent_notes: Reviewer request taken: the commentary now says that פִּתְאֹם (v. 5, defective) and פִּתְאוֹם (v. 8, full vav) are the same adverb, both with alef. The earlier text had it wrong.

וַיֹּרֵם is a vav-consecutive imperfect ('and he shot'). Radak and Meiri say the past stands for the future, the usual manner of prophecy; the English versions (KJV, ASV, BBE, Webster) use the future or present. The literal layer keeps the Hebrew past form; the dramatic layer also uses the past, and the commentary notes the dispute. Rashi and Metzudat David read it as a past event (Daniel and the lions); I leave that midrashic frame to the commentary and do not build it into the translations.

STEPBible 'they will be' for הָיוּ is a perfect; I glossed 'they have become'. 'Wounds' (מַכּוֹתָם) is plural; Hebrew has no verb 'to be wounded', so KJV's 'shall they be wounded' recasts a noun clause as a verb.

agent_notes: The text is hard: וַיַּכְשִׁילוּהוּ has a plural verb with a singular object suffix ('and they made him stumble'), and the antecedent of 'him' is the tongue (Radak, Meiri). The KJV 'shall make their own tongue to fall upon themselves' reverses the roles. I follow the Hebrew: they, i.e. the plotters, are made to stumble, and their tongue is upon them. יִתְנֹדְדוּ is from נדד 'to wander, flee', which the KJV follows ('flee away'). The ASV 'wag the head' follows Rashi's and Metzudat David's gloss of shaking the head. I kept the Hebrew's single image of shuddering and shaking, and flagged both readings.
